pages.x: Slavery was old in Africa, Europe and the Middle East. But when the sugar, tobacco and silver of the Americas needed workers, and the native peoples were dying, Europeans began to buy captives in West Africa and ship them across the Atlantic. From the 1520s ships sailed straight from Africa to the Americas.

Most captives were taken in wars and raids between African states, or kidnapped, and sold at the coast to European traders for cloth, guns, iron and cowrie shells. Kingdoms such as Dahomey and Asante grew rich and strong on the trade.

On the crossing, the Middle Passage, captives were chained below decks, packed so tightly they could barely move, for six to ten weeks. About one in seven died at sea, of disease, hunger and despair. Some leapt overboard.

In 1788 campaigners against the trade printed a plan of the slave ship Brookes, showing how 454 people could be packed into its hold under British law. It became one of the most famous images of the campaign.

Olaudah Equiano said he was kidnapped as a boy in what is now Nigeria and shipped to the Caribbean. He bought his own freedom, and his life story, published in London in 1789, made thousands of readers see the trade through the eyes of its victims.

Most enslaved Africans went to Brazil and the Caribbean to grow sugar, in such brutal conditions that many were worked to death within a few years. About 400,000 were taken to North America. Their children were born slaves too.

Enslaved people resisted from the start: they ran away, rose in revolts such as the one that freed Haiti, and kept their cultures alive. In Britain a mass campaign won a ban on the trade in 1807. The last known slave ship reached Cuba in 1867, and Brazil freed its last slaves in 1888.

The trade was one of the largest forced migrations in history. It built fortunes in Europe and the Americas, held back West Africa, and left a racism whose effects last today. It also made the African diaspora, whose music, faiths and food shaped the whole Atlantic world.
